titulo_es: Numbers, dates and time (numbers, dates and time)
descripcion_es: Counting, saying prices, times, days of the week and months.
resumen: Vocabulary for counting, saying prices, asking and telling the time, and talking about days, months and dates.

explicacion.texto: Be careful with pairs that sound similar: thirteen (13) / thirty (30), fifteen (15) / fifty (50). In -teen the stress is at the end; in -ty, at the beginning. In British English you put and before the tens and units: one hundred and twenty (120).

filas: My birthday is on the third of May.
exactly on the hour (es: en punto)
15 minutes after / 15 minutes before the hour (es: y cuarto / menos cuarto)
30 minutes after the hour (es: y media)
The train leaves at half past two.
at (time) / on (day) / in (month, year) (es: a / el / en)
at 8, on Monday, in June, in 2025
before midday / after midday (es: de la mañana / de la tarde-noche)
the seven days of the week (es: lunes … domingo)
the twelve months of the year (es: enero … diciembre)
We go on holiday in August.
Saturday and Sunday (es: el fin de semana)
What do you do at the weekend?
this day / the next day / the day before (es: hoy / mañana / ayer)
in two days' time (es: pasado mañana)
The exam is the day after tomorrow.
asking the date (es: ¿A qué fecha estamos?)

items: Days and months are written with a capital letter: Monday, April.
Dates are said with an ordinal number: the 4th of July / July the 4th.
Decimals use a point: 3.5 = three point five.
Years are read in pairs: 1998 = nineteen ninety-eight; 2025 = twenty twenty-five.

ejemplos.frase: The museum opens at ten o'clock on Sundays.
ejemplos.traduccion: El museo abre a las diez en punto los domingos.

ejemplos.frase: My daughter was born on the 21st of March.
ejemplos.traduccion: Mi hija nació el 21 de marzo.

ejemplos.frase: It's quarter past eight; we're late!
ejemplos.traduccion: Son las ocho y cuarto; ¡llegamos tarde!

ejemplos.frase: Three coffees, please. – That's six fifty.
ejemplos.traduccion: Tres cafés, por favor. – Son seis cincuenta.

ejemplos.frase: There are thirty days in September.
I'll call you the day after tomorrow.

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: With days of the week, use on.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: It's monday, the five of may.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: It's Monday, the fifth of May.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Days and months with a capital letter, and dates with an ordinal number.
Hundred, thousand and million do not take -s after a number.
The time is said with past and to.

ejercicios.explicacion: The table sums up the prepositions of time: at with times, on with days and in with months and years. The clue is Thursday, a day of the week, which needs on. Spanish “el jueves” has no preposition, so learners tend to leave it out or use in. Remember also that days are written with a capital letter.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With days of the week, use on.

errores_previstos.explicacion: In is used with months and years; with days of the week, use on.
At is used with times; with days of the week it is on.
A calque of Spanish “el jueves”: in English there is no article, but the preposition on.

ejercicios.explicacion: According to the table, with months you use in: in June, in November. The clue is November, which is a month and not a specific date. If the exact day were given, the preposition would change: on the 5th of November. The month is written with a capital letter.

errores_previstos.explicacion: On is used with days and specific dates; with a month on its own, use in.
At is used with times; with months it is in.

ejercicios.explicacion: According to the table, with times you use at: at 8, at 9:30. The clue is the time 9:30. Spanish “a las nueve y media” makes you think of to or in, but in English the preposition for times is always at.

errores_previstos.explicacion: In is used with months, years or parts of the day; with a specific time it is at.
On is used with days; with times it is at.
A calque of Spanish “a las”; in English the time goes with at.

ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes “quarter past / quarter to”, “15 minutes after / 15 minutes before the hour”. The clue is 7:45: there are fifteen minutes to go until eight, so you use to with the next hour, eight. Just as in Spanish we say “las ocho menos cuarto”, English counts towards the coming hour.

por_opcion.quarter to eight: Correct. 7:45 is fifteen minutes before eight: quarter to eight.

ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes “half past”, “30 minutes after the hour”. The clue is 4:30: thirty minutes have passed since four, so you use past with the hour that has already begun. In informal British English you also hear “half four” with the same meaning (4:30). “Half to” does not exist.

por_opcion.half to four: Incorrect. “Half to” does not exist in English: the half hour is always said with past.

ejercicios.frase: There are ___ people in the city.
ejercicios.explicacion: The typical mistakes on the card warn that hundred, thousand and million do not take -s after a number: two million people. The clue is three, a specific number before it. You do not add of either, unlike Spanish “millones de”. You only say millions of when there is no number: millions of people.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Million takes neither -s nor of after a number.
ejercicios.traduccion: En la ciudad hay tres millones de habitantes.

por_opcion.three million: Correct. After a number, million takes neither -s nor of: three million people.
por_opcion.three millions: Incorrect. Million does not take -s when it comes after a number.
por_opcion.three millions of: Incorrect. It is a calque of Spanish “tres millones de”; after a number there is neither -s nor of.

ejercicios.explicacion: The card says that dates are said with an ordinal number: the 4th of July. The clue is the structure “the ___ of June”, which needs an ordinal. In compound numbers only the last part becomes ordinal: twenty-two becomes twenty-second. So you say “the twenty-second of June”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Dates are said with an ordinal number: twenty-second.

por_opcion.twenty-second: Correct. It is the ordinal of 22: only the last part changes (second).
por_opcion.twenty-two: Incorrect. It is the cardinal number; in dates you use the ordinal.
por_opcion.twentieth-two: Incorrect. It does not exist: in compounds only the last part becomes ordinal.

ejercicios.enunciado: Write the ordinal number of 3 in words.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes “first, second, third”, “1st, 2nd, 3rd”. The first three ordinals are irregular; from fourth onwards you add -th. The clue is floor, which is counted with ordinals, as in Spanish. The ordinal of three is third.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The ordinal of three is third.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Third is irregular; it is not formed by adding -th to three.
This is the cardinal number; for a floor you use the ordinal third.
Spelling mistake: it is spelt third.

ejercicios.frase: How ___ is this bag? – It's thirty euros.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes “How much is it?”, for asking the price. The clue is the answer, “It's thirty euros”: the question is about a price, and you ask about money with much. Many is used for countable things (how many bags), not for the price.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To ask the price: How much is…?
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Cuánto cuesta este bolso? – Cuesta treinta euros.

errores_previstos.explicacion: How many asks about a number of things; for the price, use how much.
“How cost is” does not exist; say How much is…? or How much does it cost?

ejercicios.explicacion: The typical mistakes on the card include “See you in Monday” versus “on Monday”: with days of the week, use on. The clue is Monday. Both on Monday (this Monday) and on Mondays (every Monday) are accepted, because both are correct and only the idea of habit changes.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With days of the week, use on.
ejercicios.traduccion: Empiezo a trabajar el lunes (los lunes).

errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: with days of the week, use on.
At is used with times; with days it is on.
A calque of Spanish “el lunes”: in English there is no article, but the preposition on.

ejercicios.frase: It's twenty and five past three.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that the time is said with past and to, and the correction shows that the minutes are said as a single number. The clue is “twenty and five”, a calque of Spanish “veinte y cinco”: in English 25 is twenty-five, usually with a hyphen. The result is “It's twenty-five past three”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The minutes are said as a single number: twenty-five past.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It's twenty and five past three.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: numbers do not take and between the tens and units; it is twenty-five.
A calque of Spanish “las tres y veinticinco”; in English you say twenty-five past three.
To means “before the hour”: it would be 2:35, not 3:25.

ejercicios.frase: The course costs two hundreds euros.
respuestas: The course costs two hundred euros.
ejercicios.explicacion: The typical mistakes on the card remind you that hundred, thousand and million do not take -s after a number. The clue is two, before hundreds. The correction is “two hundred euros”. Hundreds only appears with no number before it: hundreds of euros (Spanish “cientos de euros”).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Hundred does not take -s after a number.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The course costs two hundreds euros.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: after a number, hundred does not take -s.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The course costs two hundreds of euros.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It adds a calque of Spanish “de”; after a number there is neither -s nor of.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The course cost two hundred euros.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It corrects the number but changes the verb: with the course you need costs, in the third person.

ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes “What time is it?”, for asking the time. It is a fixed question: What time at the beginning, then the verb is and the subject it, because in questions with be the verb goes before the subject. Spanish has no explicit subject, but in English it is compulsory.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The question for the time is What time is it?

errores_previstos.explicacion: That order is only used in indirect questions (Do you know what time it is?); in a direct question it is What time is it.
What time goes together, as a single question phrase.

ejercicios.frase: The exam is the day after ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table includes “the day after tomorrow”, “in two days' time”. The clue is “the day after”: tomorrow is missing. “The day before yesterday” (Spanish “anteayer”) is formed in the same way.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “pasado mañana” is the day after tomorrow.

errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of Spanish “mañana” in the sense of part of the day; Spanish “pasado mañana” is the day after tomorrow.
Spelling mistake: it is spelt tomorrow, with double r.

ejercicios.explicacion: According to the table, with years you use in: in 2025. The clue is 1948, a year. Remember also that years are read in pairs: nineteen forty-eight. “Be born” means to come into the world and goes in the past: was born.

por_opcion.in: Correct. With years, use in: in 1948.
por_opcion.on: Incorrect. On is used with days and specific dates, not with a year on its own.
por_opcion.at: Incorrect. At is used with times, not with years.

descripcion_larga_es: This card brings together the basics for handling figures and time in English: cardinal and ordinal numbers, prices, the time, days, months and dates, with the prepositions at, on and in. It is everyday vocabulary and appears in any practical conversation. Spanish speakers find it hard to tell the time with past and to, to use ordinals in dates, to write days and months with capital letters and to remember that hundred or million do not take -s.

contexto.que_es: It is the vocabulary for counting, saying prices, asking and telling the time, and talking about days, months, years and dates. It includes cardinal numbers (one, two) and ordinal numbers (first, second), the expressions for telling the time (half past, quarter to) and the prepositions of time at, on and in.
contexto.por_que_importa: It is used every day: arranging an appointment, shopping, catching a train or understanding a timetable. A mistake with the time or the date can make you miss a meeting, and confusing thirteen with thirty changes a figure. It is the basis for talking about data and statistics at higher levels later on.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: It comes up when asking prices (How much is it?), arranging to meet (on Thursday at 9:30), and talking about birthdays or historical dates. Spanish speakers tend to say “in Monday”, “the five of May”, “two hundreds” or “ten and a quarter”, calques of Spanish that English resolves with on, ordinal numbers, hundred without -s and quarter past.
